summary: Learners estimate values from plotted linear and quadratic graphs using a consistent 'up-and-across' reading routine: state the axis scale first, find the given value on one axis, travel to the graph, then across to read the other axis. Reading is inherently approximate — report to a sensible interval, not false precision. Treat x-axis crossings as approximate solutions of f(x)=0 (a parabola has two, one, or none), and the intersection of two graphs as a value satisfying both. Real-world graphs (distance–time, cost) are read for contextual quantities with attention to units and realistic range.
misconceptions: Reads against the wrong scale (assumes each square is one unit) or reads off the wrong axis.
Gives a single false-precise value instead of an estimate to a sensible interval.
Stops at the first x-axis crossing, missing a parabola's second root.
Confuses where a single line crosses an AXIS with where two graphs intersect each other.

activities.title: Up-and-across reading with the scale stated first
steps: Before reading anything, state aloud what one grid square represents on each axis (e.g. 'each square is 1 unit' or 'each square is 2 units').
For a plotted curve, draw a line up from a given x-value to the curve, then across to the y-axis, and record the estimated y.
Read a value to the nearest sensible fraction of a grid square, writing it as a band (e.g. 'between 2 and 2.5, about 2.25') rather than a single over-precise figure.
Re-read the same physical point after the grid interval changes (e.g. squares now worth 2) and note how the number changes while the point does not.
activities.insight: A read-off value depends on the axis scale, so checking the scale comes before trusting any number; a value between grid lines is an estimate given to a sensible interval, not an exact figure.

activities.title: Finding both roots of a parabola
steps: On a parabola such as y = x² − 4, find every x-value where the curve meets the x-axis (where height = 0), not just the first one encountered.

Use the symmetry of the curve: after finding one crossing, look on the opposite branch for its partner (a parabola that only touches the x-axis at its vertex has just one, and one that never reaches the x-axis has none).
Given a target height (e.g. y = 5), find both symmetric x-values that reach it, and read each as an estimate.
Distinguish 'y = 0' (where the curve meets the x-axis) from the y-intercept (where the curve meets the y-axis, here −4).
activities.insight: 'Find where y = 0' can have two answers for a parabola, located symmetrically; stopping at the first crossing misses a root, and the x-axis crossings are different from the y-intercept.

activities.title: Intersections as shared solutions, and checking read-offs
steps: Read the intersection point of two plotted graphs (e.g. a curve and the line y = x) as the value(s) satisfying both.
Distinguish where a single line crosses an axis from where two graphs cross each other.

After reading a solution from a graph, substitute it back to check that it approximately satisfies the equation(s) (both sides come out close, not necessarily exactly equal), especially when the plot may be inaccurately drawn.
Interpret a real-world graph (e.g. distance–time) to answer a contextual question, stating units and sense-checking against a realistic range.
activities.insight: An intersection of two graphs gives the value(s) common to both; a graphical read-off is approximate and can be wrong if the plot is inaccurate, so solutions should be checked and sense-checked against context.

checkQuestion: Here is the graph of y = x² − 4, drawn on axes where each square is one unit. Using the graph and showing your reading lines each time: (a) what is y when x = 2.5? (b) for which values of x is y = 0? (c) roughly what is x when y = 5?
checkAnswer: (a) y ≈ 2.25 (read up from x = 2.5 to the curve, then across — about 2.2–2.3). (b) x = −2 AND x = 2 — both crossings of the x-axis. (c) x ≈ 3 and x ≈ −3 — the curve reaches height 5 on both branches. Values are read as estimates to a sensible interval, using the stated scale.
